entries.name: Hidden Markov random field
entries.definition: A latent-variable graphical-model family whose unobserved label field has the Markov property on a specified neighborhood graph, with observations conditionally independent across sites given the labels and each depending only on its corresponding hidden state.
entries.identity_notes: The classical independent-emission construction specifies a hidden label field X and observed field Y, rather than only a generic MRF. It is a restricted hidden–observed pair Markov field: its hidden prior must retain the stated graph and its conditional observation law factors by site. A chain-shaped hidden graph recovers an ordinary HMM, but general spatial graphs are not subtypes of sequential Markov chains. A Gaussian observation distribution does not make the discrete hidden label field a continuous Gaussian random field. This model identity is separate from Gibbs sampling, ICM, EM and the paper’s HMRF-EM fitting framework. limitations: The finite-state Gibbs prior needs a finite positive partition function, and emissions must be normalized with valid support. Gaussian emissions require positive variance. Conditional independence is a modeling restriction, not a demonstrated property of every image or downsampled observation.

The report’s Equation(2) gives independence across paired sites for its finite-mixture setup; applying that product to an interacting HMRF would discard the defining label dependencies. The later Equation(8) and Section2.3 joint factorization specify the supported HMRF model.

The expanded Gaussian likelihood on PDF p.8 contains a quadratic-sign inconsistency. Equation(18) gives the consistent negative log-emission energy. Figure5 step4 adds likelihood and prior although MAP requires their product, or a sum of log terms as in Equation(14). These printed algorithm displays are not certified implementations.

The report’s fitted HMRF-EM uses ICM-estimated neighboring labels in local responsibilities. Those plug-in responsibilities generally differ from exact full-field posterior marginals. Ideal EM monotonicity and exact global MAP are not guaranteed for this approximation. ICM can stop at a local optimum; initialization, empty classes and vanishing Gaussian variances require care.

The bias-field correction framework adds assumptions and alternating updates beyond the generic model. A positive multiplicative bias before logarithms and an additive log-bias must be distinguished. No clinical validity, universal segmentation advantage, runtime guarantee or author-code reproduction is asserted.

The inspected source is the 20-page FMRIB technical report TR00YZ1, not the later 2001 journal article. Its self-description as novel does not establish first invention; earlier hidden-field literature and the existing pair-field record supply historical context.

claims.statement: On a finite graph, choose a proper hidden prior p(x)=Z^(-1)*exp(-sum_c V_c(x_c)) and normalized site emission laws b_i(y_i|x_i). Their joint law is p(x,y)=p(x)*product_i b_i(y_i|x_i). At fixed observed y with positive evidence, p(x|y) is proportional to the same clique prior times the local emission factors. Its negative log density is the prior energy plus sum_i[-log b_i(y_i|x_i)] up to a constant, preserving the hidden neighborhood graph. A local conditional label update conditions on neighboring hidden labels and the local observation. A site posterior marginal instead sums over all other labels given the complete observation field. With independent hidden labels and common class weights the model reduces to independent finite-mixture observations. MAP estimates a joint labeling. In loopy graphs these inference objectives need not admit the exact noniterative recursions available for a tree.

entries.name: Hidden Markov tree
entries.definition: A latent-variable model on a fixed rooted tree in which hidden states factor into a root distribution and conditionally independent parent-to-child transitions, with observations emitted independently by their corresponding hidden states.
entries.identity_notes: This record uses the classical independent-emission meaning of hidden Markov tree, exemplified by the inspected quadtree image model. The tree describes stochastic dependencies between sites or scales; it is not a decision tree, a hierarchical mixture-of-experts gate tree or the within-time hierarchy of a hidden Markov decision tree. It is a restricted pairwise Markov tree with kernels A(x_child|x_parent)*b(y_child|x_child). Some pairwise-tree literature uses hidden Markov tree more broadly for a Markov hidden marginal with correlated observations; that broader usage is not equated with this independent-emission definition. A path is an HMM special case; branching is permitted. limitations: The record is scoped to independent child transitions and independent site emissions on a fixed finite rooted tree. Coupled siblings, loopy graphs, correlated emissions and learned topology require additional constructions. A causal tree factorization here expresses conditional probability, not intervention semantics.

Generic dense transitions with K hidden states require O(number_of_edges*K^2) arithmetic for the sum-product pass; linearity in sites assumes a fixed state count. Source complexity statements linear in K are not adopted for arbitrary dense kernels. Positive evidence and careful support handling are required; numerical scaling reduces but does not eliminate all numerical risks.

The source’s Equation(10) omits the complement needed for a minimized Hamming loss, and Figure4 prints argmin where Equation(11) correctly uses argmax of a posterior. Its preliminary prior pass requires root-to-leaf order. This record uses consistent sum-product/max-product semantics rather than those literal displays.

For Equation(17)’s shared same-state transition probability theta, the unconstrained EM update is expected same-state edge count divided by edge count. Equations(26)–(27) print an extra state-count divisor, conflicting with the earlier theta>1/K restriction. Active parameter constraints, zero expected counts and emission degeneracy need separate treatment.

The exact posterior factorization in Equation(29) supports ancestral sampling after subtree messages. The experimental H-MCEM uses a local-observation conditioning shortcut and constructed coarse observations; those samples are not certified exact draws from the original posterior. SMAP is a different loss with an approximate procedure, not an alias for exact joint MAP or MPM.

Quadtree image priors can create location-dependent block artifacts. EM remains initialization-sensitive and need not find a global optimum. The selected synthetic, flood and microscopy examples establish application context, not universal segmentation superiority, a modern benchmark or a reproduced implementation.

claims.statement: Specify a normalized root law pi(x_r), normalized transitions A_s(x_s|x_parent(s)) and normalized local emissions b_s(y_s|x_s). Then p(x,y)=pi(x_r)*product_nonroot A_s*product_s b_s. At a site without an observation use emission factor1. For finite hidden states, an upward likelihood message is L_s(x_s)=b_s(y_s|x_s)*product_child_t sum_(x_t) A_t(x_t|x_s)*L_t(x_t). The root posterior is proportional to pi*L_r, and each child posterior conditional is proportional to A_t*L_t for fixed parent. Propagating the root posterior downward gives node and edge marginals. Replacing child sums with maxima and retaining maximizing states yields joint MAP by backtracking; independently maximizing node marginals gives MPM and can select a different configuration. Exact node and edge posterior expectations permit an EM parameter update for a specified, properly normalized tree model. The source instantiates the tree as a quadtree, with optional observation levels and optional parameter tying across scales.

entries.name: Iterative conditional estimation
entries.definition: An incomplete-data parameter-estimation procedure that repeatedly replaces a chosen complete-data estimator by its conditional expectation given observed data under the current parameter estimate.
entries.identity_notes: ICE specifies expectation of an estimator, not maximization of an expected complete-data log likelihood as in EM. The estimator may be maximum likelihood, least squares or another supported complete-data estimator. Shared applications to hidden Markov models do not make ICE a model family, an ICM label optimizer or a synonym for every stochastic EM method. Its behavior depends on the selected estimator and parameterization. The short acronym is scoped to this estimation procedure. Short acronyms were included in the complete normalized identity comparison. The absence assessment is bounded to the pin, native collection and inspected semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The complete-data estimator must be defined on posterior-supported completed data and have the required moments. Empty mixture components, boundary or infinite MLEs, constrained parameter spaces and nonidentifiability need explicit conventions; a conditional mean can leave a nonconvex parameter space.

Conditional expectation is the least-squares approximation to an integrable squared-error target under a fixed law. That fact does not prove decreasing true parameter error, observed-likelihood monotonicity or global convergence across ICE iterations with changing laws.

The Delmas equivalence uses the mean/expectation parameter psi, although the source calls it canonical; its natural parameter phi is distinct. The claim is not automatic for arbitrary coordinates, curved/constrained exponential families or boundary estimates. A nonlinear transformation does not generally commute with conditional expectation.

For Gaussian mixtures, expectation of a complete-data class mean or variance containing a random class count differs in general from a ratio of expected sufficient statistics. The usual Gaussian-parameter ICE update therefore cannot simply be replaced by an EM update without checking the conditions.

Monte Carlo approximation requires valid posterior sampling and appropriate convergence conditions. Correlated Gibbs samples, finite sample counts and apparently steady parameters do not by themselves certify exact expectations or convergence. A one-sample version can resemble stochastic EM for a specific complete-data estimator; it is not every stochastic-approximation EM algorithm.

The inspected examples in Delmas contain scaling/covariance notation issues, and its introductory suggestion that mixed discrete-continuous data make likelihood irrelevant is not adopted. The definition and qualified coordinate comparison do not certify all printed example formulas. Neither inspected paper provides a universal empirical performance guarantee; no fitting, benchmark or author-code run was performed.

claims.statement: Let observed data be y and hidden data h, and choose a complete-data estimator T(h,y) of a parameter theta. From a valid current theta_k, set theta_(k+1)=E_(theta_k)[T(H,y)|Y=y], when this expectation exists and remains admissible. A finite hidden space permits a posterior-weighted sum; otherwise average T over appropriate posterior samples as a Monte Carlo approximation. This average is taken after evaluating the estimator on each completed datum. It generally differs from applying a nonlinear estimator to expected sufficient statistics. With a complete-data maximum-likelihood estimator, ICE averages an argmax, whereas EM takes an argmax after averaging the log likelihood. For a regular full identifiable exponential family with a valid finite interior complete-data MLE and an invertible mean-parameter map, the expectation coordinate psi=E_theta[s(H,Y)] has complete-data estimator s(H,Y), so ICE and EM coincide in that coordinate. Nonlinear reparameterization need not preserve equality of their updates.

mapping_assessment: HMRF has a related ProbabilisticGraphicalModel mapping because the pinned class is defined and parented as a machine-learning task. The independent-emission HMT has a broad BayesianNetwork mapping: a rooted hidden tree with emitted observation leaves is a restricted normalized directed acyclic probability model, without causal-intervention semantics. SpatialRegression and RegressionAnalysis are regression-scoped, not generic latent-label models or incomplete-data estimators. GaussianNoiseLayer, GaussianDropoutLayer, HiddenLayer and ProbabilisticHiddenLayer are neural components. MaximumLayer is an elementwise tensor merger, not MAP, EM or ICE. Native MRF, HMM, paired field, triplet field, paired tree, EM, HME and HMDT distinguish generic graph scope, hidden-observed partition, topology, augmentation, estimator iteration and gating. For a finite site set and specified undirected neighborhood graph, assign clique energies phi_c(x_c,y_c) and define p(x,y)=Z^(-1)*exp(-sum_c phi_c(x_c,y_c)), with a finite positive partition function. At fixed complete y, the posterior p(x|y) retains clique factors on the same graph; fixing x likewise gives a local conditional observation field. Summing over one field can introduce dependencies beyond that graph, so neither p(x) nor p(y) is required to retain its Markov structure. A classical hidden Markov field p(x)*product_s b_(x_s)(y_s) is recovered by selecting label-clique and site-emission energies. This construction permits spatially correlated observation models without separately specifying a conditional likelihood whose configuration-dependent normalization could destroy locality of the label posterior. Local conditional probabilities support Gibbs sampling of hidden labels and approximation of sitewise posterior marginals; preserving the exact model factorization does not make finite sampling exact. Limitations: The definition presupposes a proper joint distribution. For the continuous Gaussian examples, each hidden configuration needs a positive-definite observation precision matrix and a finite joint partition function; positive single-site conditional variances alone do not ensure this. The source’s Gaussian displays contain normalization, completed-square and variance inconsistencies. For a local energy alpha+beta*y+delta*y^2 with delta>0, integrating exp(-energy) gives sqrt(pi/delta)*exp(-alpha+beta^2/(4*delta)); its conditional mean is -beta/(2*delta) and variance is 1/(2*delta). Off-diagonal precision makes inverse diagonal precision differ from marginal variance. This record does not certify the printed Gaussian sampling implementation. The first eight-neighbor example requires particular caution: under unit diagonal precision and -0.2 on each unordered neighbor edge, a 4-by-4 open grid has a negative constant-vector quadratic form. This is a curator calculation under explicit counting and boundary conventions, not a claim about uninspected author code. Posterior Markov structure is not a guarantee of efficient exact inference on a loopy field, Gibbs mixing, parameter identifiability or a globally optimal segmentation. Per-site marginal modes and a joint maximum-probability configuration are different objectives. Section 5 leaves observation-only parameter estimation through iterative conditional estimation as future work. The synthetic texture illustrations and inconsistent sampling-count caption do not support a universal performance claim. For level m and time t, its latent decision z_t^m is distributed conditional on the current input x_t, all current ancestor decisions z_t^1,...,z_t^(m-1), and its own preceding decision z_(t-1)^m. Initial decisions condition on the input and current ancestors without a preceding-time state. Multiplying these normalized conditional factors and one observation factor p(y_t|x_t,z_t^1,...,z_t^M) per time gives a normalized directed model conditional on inputs. A latent path through the hierarchy selects an output expert. Exact inference may enumerate the joint states but grows exponentially with hierarchy depth. The paper explores three distinct approximations: a product of chain-path distributions that preserves temporal dependence within each level; a product over times of tree-structured distributions that preserves current ancestor dependence; and a point-mass path approximation. Its point-mass procedure optimizes one level’s path by a Viterbi subroutine while holding the other paths fixed. These are inference choices for the family, not alternative definitions of its identity. Limitations: Same-level temporal connections and current-ancestor dependencies are defining restrictions of the inspected construction. They do not cover arbitrary cross-time connections or all models whose names contain hidden Markov tree. The probabilistic hierarchy sums over decision paths; it is not necessarily a hard classification tree. Input conditioning and an output expert do not imply a causal interpretation of the graph. Independent latent chains, a single HMM and an ordinary hierarchical mixture arise under specific restrictions, not as unconditional aliases of this family. Forest-of-chains, forest-of-trees and point-mass inference discard different posterior dependencies. A coordinate Viterbi step finds the best path for one fixed-context chain, not a guaranteed global joint MAP path. The paper motivates hierarchical time scales but its synthetic runs did not always recover the intended hierarchy. No universal coarse-to-fine organization, general convergence guarantee, benchmark advantage or author-code reproduction is asserted. A latent path through the hierarchy selects an output expert. Exact inference may enumerate the joint states but grows exponentially with hierarchy depth. These are inference choices for the family, not alternative definitions of its identity.

GaussianNoiseLayer, GaussianDropoutLayer, HiddenLayer and ProbabilisticHiddenLayer are neural components. MaximumLayer is an elementwise tensor merger, not MAP, EM or ICE. Native MRF, HMM, paired field, triplet field, paired tree, EM, HME and HMDT distinguish generic graph scope, hidden-observed partition, topology, augmentation, estimator iteration and gating.
